I've been a loyal T-Mobile customer since 2016, when they launched the T-Mobile ONE plan. Although I've always enjoyed the military discount, with T-Mobile's price hikes, my monthly bill eventually climbed to $113. I'd had enough, so I started looking for cheaper alternatives. On top of that, Apple's iPhone 18 Pro is at least $100 more expensive this year, so I figured if I'm going to switch phones, cutting my monthly bill might help offset the cost. That's why I started shopping around for MVNOs.

What is an MVNO?

MVNO stands for "Mobile Virtual Network Operator." Simply put, an MVNO is a wireless carrier that doesn't own its own nationwide cellular network. Instead, it buys network access from one of the major carriers (AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon) and resells that service to its own customers. Think of them as middlemen for wireless service.

That means switching to an MVNO doesn't necessarily mean giving up the network you already use. For example, Mint Mobile uses T-Mobile's network, Visible uses Verizon's network, and US Mobile lets customers choose between all three major networks. In this article, I'll focus on these three MVNOs because they're the ones I researched most thoroughly before leaving T-Mobile, but there are plenty of other options out there.

In short, an MVNO gives you another way to buy cellular service without going directly to the company that owns the network.

Why are MVNOs cheaper? And what's the catch?

If MVNOs use the same cellular networks as AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon, how can they charge so much less? The simple answer is that MVNOs don't have to bear all the costs of running a nationwide wireless carrier. They don't have to build and maintain their own networks, many operate primarily online without physical retail stores, and they have relatively fewer employees. The savings can be passed on to customers through lower monthly fees.

MVNO plans tend to be simpler, without all the "perks" and add-ons that traditional carriers love to bundle in. Depending on the carrier and plan, you may not get free streaming subscriptions or other customer-retention sweeteners. But the money you save with an MVNO can easily more than cover the cost of subscribing to those "free" perks on your own.

That was exactly my situation. I always looked forward to the free MLB.TV subscription T-Mobile included and used it every baseball season. But I never watch Netflix, so the "Netflix on Us" perk was completely wasted on me. Even if I wanted both Netflix and MLB.TV, I could pay for those subscriptions myself and still come out ahead with what I save by switching. My goal is simple: I want reliable, reasonably priced cellular service, and I don't need T-Mobile to throw in a bunch of extras to earn my business.

The "catch" isn't necessarily worse service—it's that when you pay less, you get less. What exactly you give up depends on the MVNO and plan you choose. Video streaming may be limited to lower resolution, high-speed or prioritized data allowances will vary, and network priority may differ. I have fast Wi-Fi at home and rarely go to "busy" places like concerts or stadiums, so network priority doesn't make much of a difference in my day-to-day use. But I do travel internationally from time to time, so international data is an important consideration for me. Some MVNOs include international data and texting, while others charge extra or have more limited coverage outside the U.S.

There are some less obvious differences too, especially when buying a new iPhone. If you choose an MVNO as your carrier, you can't take advantage of Apple Card monthly installments or the iPhone Upgrade Program. To use either of those options, you'd have to stick with AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon. In practice, that means if you want to buy your iPhone directly from Apple, you'll basically have to pay full price. The major carriers can also offer substantial trade-in credits and other promotions, which generally aren't available through MVNOs. Apple Watch support isn't universal either, so if you use a cellular-enabled Apple Watch, that's something to look into.

Finally, most MVNOs rely primarily on phone and online customer support rather than staffed retail locations where you can talk to someone face-to-face. I consider myself fairly tech-savvy, and I don't enjoy waiting in line at a store for help anyway. In my experience, the salespeople in those stores end up calling the same customer support line I could call from home, so it really isn't a drawback for me.

Most importantly, none of these limitations are universal across all MVNOs. Different carriers and plans come with different terms, so it's worth understanding exactly what you'd be getting before making the switch.

Three MVNOs worth considering

After committing to leaving T-Mobile, I started looking for alternatives. Verizon's and AT&T's postpaid plans were even more expensive than what I was already paying, so those other two major carriers were out. I ultimately narrowed my search down to US Mobile, Mint Mobile, and Visible. Each had something that appealed to me, and all could significantly lower my monthly bill while still letting me use a major carrier's network.

US Mobile is arguably the most flexible of the three, and it's the carrier I ultimately switched to from T-Mobile. That doesn't necessarily mean it's the best fit for you, or even the best MVNO of the three—it just happened to be the right choice for me.

US Mobile wasn't actually my first pick originally; I only learned about the company while researching MVNOs. But the more I looked into it, the more it stood out. Here's why: US Mobile offers service on all three major U.S. networks, so customers can choose whichever one works best for them. It also has a Multi-Network add-on feature that can activate two networks on the same iPhone simultaneously, without an extra number. Both networks are tied to the same line, and your iPhone can use whichever one has a better connection for calls and data. So if T-Mobile's network works great at your office but Verizon's is better at home, you can take advantage of both without carrying two phones or managing two numbers. US Mobile charges extra for this feature, which I don't personally need, but it's nice that it's available.

I recently moved and was curious how Verizon's coverage near my new home compared to T-Mobile's, so I decided to test both networks. I set up my wife's iPhone on US Mobile's Light Speed network (which is T-Mobile) and mine on Warp (which is Verizon) so we could compare firsthand. Verizon turned out to be noticeably better in our area, so switching to US Mobile was a real win: better coverage and a much lower monthly bill.

Mint Mobile was actually my original first choice because it's owned by T-Mobile, meaning I could stick with the network I already knew, but at a much lower price. What I didn't like was that it doesn't include international data. My wife and I love going on cruises, and travel is a big part of our lives, so having cellular data outside the U.S. is important to us. Mint does offer international data, but you have to pay extra for it, and that would quickly eat into the savings. I also wasn't a fan of having to pay taxes and fees on top.

Visible is similarly straightforward, but it only uses Verizon's network. My biggest concern with Visible was Verizon's coverage in my area. I'd been a T-Mobile customer for nearly a decade and knew exactly how T-Mobile's network performed, but I had no idea what Verizon's coverage was like. That was the main reason I ultimately chose US Mobile over Visible—US Mobile let me try out Verizon's network, and if it didn't work out, I still had T-Mobile and AT&T as options. Visible's top unlimited plan also includes free cellular Apple Watch service, which is appealing. (US Mobile's top plan, if you use its Warp—which is Verizon's network—offers the same perk.)

What you need to switch

Switching to an MVNO was easier than I expected. My wife and I kept our existing iPhones, and transferring both lines from T-Mobile to US Mobile took only about ten minutes—I didn't even have to get off the couch. You need an unlocked, compatible iPhone (or Android phone, but I'm mainly talking iPhones here) and some information from your current carrier. If you want to keep your existing phone number, just don't cancel your old service before the number transfer goes through.

Here's what you need to switch:

  • Your current carrier's account number
  • Your transfer PIN
  • An unlocked, compatible iPhone
  • A new eSIM
  • A little patience

I pre-paid US Mobile for a full year of two unlimited data lines in preparation for the switch. My wife doesn't use a cellular Apple Watch and doesn't care about video quality, so she went with US Mobile's Unlimited Starter plan, which saved her $100 compared to the Unlimited Premium plan I chose. Two lines plus Apple Watch service for $500 a year, compared to $1,356 a year for two lines with no Apple Watch service on T-Mobile—it's a much better deal. (Again, that price already includes the military discount!)

Getting the transfer PIN from T-Mobile was straightforward—I expected to have to dig around for it somewhere, but it was no trouble at all. The steps for Verizon and AT&T are here.

After connecting my iPhone to Wi-Fi, US Mobile emailed me a new eSIM, and installing it was as simple as clicking a button in the email and following the prompts. My wife's iPhone followed the same process. The only extra step was setting up the Apple Watch, which was a breeze through US Mobile's app.

Why I'm sticking with an MVNO

Same coverage, much lower monthly bill: the savings easily outweigh what I've given up. I have fast Wi-Fi at home, so cellular data isn't as critical for me (though in speed tests, US Mobile was just as fast as T-Mobile). What matters most to me is having a strong, reliable cellular signal when I'm away from Wi-Fi, especially for making and receiving calls and texts.

No long-term contracts: most carriers have already moved away from traditional contract plans and toward device installment plans, which effectively lock you in until the phone is paid off. I've always bought my iPhones directly from Apple because I want the freedom of an unlocked model, but I also appreciate that US Mobile, Mint, and Visible don't require contracts.

Easy to switch: most MVNOs let you pay month-to-month, so you're not tied to one carrier for the long haul. If one carrier has a great promo this month and another has a better deal next month, switching is quick and easy. Prepaid accounts also don't require a credit check, so you won't take a hit to your credit score from a carrier pulling your credit—unlike postpaid accounts, which can also deny you based on your credit history. My credit record is fine, but if I wanted to switch from T-Mobile to Verizon and have them check my credit, I'd rather not have my score dinged.

Top comment: Zach Chadwick

I started with T-Mobile in 2014. Two lines with device promo trade-in offers came to $135 a month. After price hikes, plan changes, and trade-in requirements, my bill climbed to $185.

I switched to Visible in September 2025. I picked their Pro plan and used promo code "SAVE26" to get their top plan for $33 a month for 26 months.

After my mom's trade-in deal ended, I switched her over too. They were running a half-price annual deal on their top plan at the time, so her full year of service came to just $275.

Combined, both lines cost me only $671 this year—that's four months' worth of my old T-Mobile bill.

I haven't run into any issues so far. I set up Autopay, and they don't force you to use a debit card or checking account. I'm on 5G UW about 90% of the time. Streaming in 4K has been completely smooth with no buffering or lag.

I've already started a Visible "Circle" and can invite others to join, getting $5 back per month for each line—enough to cover the bill for everyone in my circle.

Pay annually and save more: the trade-off for that flexibility is that you'll save more if you're willing to prepay for a full year. Most MVNOs offer substantial discounts on annual plans, meaning you give up some of the freedom to switch whenever you want in exchange for a lower overall price.

No surprise charges: I mentioned earlier that my wife and I love going on cruises. If you've ever forgotten to put your iPhone in airplane mode on a cruise ship, and it connects to the ship's cellular network, you know you're in for a jaw-dropping bill. With a prepaid plan, I don't have to worry about accidentally racking up massive roaming charges. If international roaming isn't included in the plan, my phone simply won't connect to networks overseas, so I won't get charged. US Mobile's plans already include taxes and fees, so the listed price is what you actually pay.

Switching to an MVNO isn't just about finding the cheapest service—it's about buying exactly what I actually want, without being forced to pay for things I don't use or need. So far, I don't feel like I've missed out on anything that matters to me (although I know I'll really miss that free MLB.TV subscription). In fact, I picked up an Apple Watch line I didn't have before, and my monthly bill is still lower. My iPhone and phone number haven't changed, and on US Mobile's Warp (Verizon) network, coverage in my area is actually better than before—and if I find an even better option down the road, I still have the freedom to switch whenever I want.

Your priorities may be different from mine, and an MVNO may not be right for everyone. But if you're paying a lot for your monthly bill right now and haven't considered an MVNO, it's worth looking into. You may be surprised at how little you'd actually be giving up.
